content: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidelines for safe abortion, recommending medical abortion using mifepristone and misoprostol or surgical abortion through vacuum aspiration or dilation and evacuation. These methods are considered both safe and effective. However, the guidelines do not include specific clinical considerations for women living with HIV. Concerns have been raised that women with HIV might face a higher risk of adverse outcomes following abortion due to factors such as immunosuppression, higher rates of co-infection with other sexually transmitted infections, and potential drug interactions between medications used for medical abortion and antiretroviral therapy. The primary goal of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of medical versus surgical abortion in women living with HIV. Secondary objectives included comparing abortion outcomes between women with and without HIV and describing the outcomes of both medical and surgical abortion specifically in women living with HIV. A comprehensive search was conducted on April 17, 2018, to identify all published and unpublished trials and observational studies related to medical and surgical abortion in women living with HIV. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched using terms related to abortion and HIV. Conference websites were also reviewed for relevant abstracts, and efforts were made to obtain unpublished data stratified by HIV status for potential analysis. The inclusion criteria for the study encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-RCTs, and observational studies. These studies needed to address one or more of the following: the effectiveness and safety of medical versus surgical abortion in women living with HIV, comparisons of abortion outcomes between women with and without HIV, or descriptions of abortion outcomes in women living with HIV. One reviewer initially screened the titles, abstracts, and citation details of the identified records. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were obtained when available. Two reviewers independently assessed these articles to determine their eligibility based on the inclusion criteria. A meta-analysis was planned if at least three studies addressed the same research question and provided comparable outcome data. Out of 3,840 records screened, only one conference abstract met the inclusion criteria. This prospective cohort study, conducted in Ukraine, evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of home administration of misoprostol for early medical abortion in women living with HIV who were less than 63 days amenorrheic. The study found that medical abortion was effective in 65 out of 68 cases (96%). The few failures included one case of incomplete abortion, one case of heavy bleeding, and one case of ongoing pregnancy. Importantly, no serious infections were reported. The authors concluded that the limited number of studies made it impossible to determine whether differences in abortion outcomes exist between women with and without HIV. However, there was no evidence to suggest that medical or surgical abortion is unsafe for women living with HIV. While further research is needed to strengthen the evidence base, healthcare providers should not hesitate to offer safe abortion services to women living with HIV.
